lessons.title: Scarcity and Choice
lessons.content: Economics studies how societies allocate scarce resources. Scarcity means there aren't enough resources to satisfy all human wants — this is the fundamental economic problem. Because of scarcity, we must make choices. Every choice has an opportunity cost — the next best alternative you give up. If you spend your money on a phone, you can't spend it on shoes — the shoes are your opportunity cost. Resources are classified as: land (natural resources), labor (human work), capital (tools, machines, buildings), and entrepreneurship (organizing the other three). Economics answers three key questions: What to produce? How to produce? For whom to produce?
examples: Opportunity cost: choosing to study instead of watching a movie — the movie is the cost
A government choosing between building a hospital or a road — it can't afford both
Land: oil, forests, water. Labor: teachers, farmers. Capital: tractors, computers. Enterprise: business owners

keyTerms.scarcity: The fundamental economic problem — limited resources vs unlimited wants
keyTerms.opportunity cost: The value of the next best alternative given up when making a choice
keyTerms.factors of production: Resources used to produce goods: land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship

quiz.question: The fundamental economic problem is:
options: Scarcity — limited resources vs unlimited wants
quiz.explanation: We can never have enough resources to satisfy all human wants — so we must choose.

quiz.question: Opportunity cost is:
options: What you give up when you make a choice
quiz.explanation: The opportunity cost is the value of the next best option you didn't choose.

quiz.question: Which is a factor of production?
quiz.explanation: The four factors are: land, labor, capital (equipment), and entrepreneurship.

lessons.title: Supply and Demand
lessons.content: Demand is the quantity of a good consumers are willing and able to buy at various prices. The law of demand: as price rises, quantity demanded falls (and vice versa). Supply is the quantity producers are willing to sell at various prices. The law of supply: as price rises, quantity supplied rises. Where supply and demand curves meet is the equilibrium — the market price. If price is above equilibrium, there's a surplus (excess supply). If price is below equilibrium, there's a shortage (excess demand). Factors that shift demand: income, tastes, price of related goods. Factors that shift supply: input costs, technology, number of producers.
examples: When smartphone prices drop, more people buy them — law of demand in action
A drought reduces coffee supply — supply curve shifts left, price rises
Equilibrium: if 1000 phones are demanded and 1000 supplied at $500, that's the market price

keyTerms.demand: The quantity of a good consumers are willing and able to buy at each price
keyTerms.supply: The quantity of a good producers are willing and able to sell at each price
keyTerms.equilibrium: The price and quantity where supply equals demand — the market clears

quiz.question: According to the law of demand, when price increases:
quiz.explanation: Higher prices make goods less affordable — fewer people buy.

quiz.question: What happens when price is below equilibrium?
quiz.explanation: Below equilibrium, demand exceeds supply — creating a shortage.

quiz.question: A drought affecting wheat would:
quiz.explanation: Less wheat available = supply decreases = price rises.

lessons.title: Economic Systems
lessons.content: Economic systems determine how resources are allocated. Market economy (capitalism): private ownership, prices set by supply and demand, minimal government intervention. Advantages: innovation, efficiency, consumer choice. Disadvantages: inequality, monopolies, market failures. Command economy (socialism/communism): government owns resources and makes all production decisions. Advantages: equality, full employment. Disadvantages: inefficiency, lack of innovation, limited freedom. Mixed economy: combines both — most modern countries are mixed. Governments provide public goods (roads, defense), regulate markets, and provide social safety nets while allowing private enterprise.
examples: Market economy: the USA — private businesses compete, prices set by markets
Command economy: North Korea — government controls all production decisions
Mixed economy: Uganda, UK, most countries — private businesses plus government services and regulation

keyTerms.market economy: An economic system where prices and production are determined by supply and demand
keyTerms.command economy: An economic system where the government controls resource allocation and production
keyTerms.mixed economy: A system combining free market elements with government intervention

quiz.question: In a market economy, prices are set by:
quiz.explanation: In a market economy, buyers and sellers determine prices through supply and demand.

quiz.question: Most modern countries have:
quiz.explanation: Most countries combine private enterprise with government regulation and services.

quiz.question: A disadvantage of a market economy is:
quiz.explanation: Free markets can create significant wealth inequality without government intervention.

lessons.title: Competition and Market Structures
lessons.content: Market structure describes how competitive a market is. Perfect competition: many small firms selling identical products — no single firm can influence price (theoretical: closest example is agricultural markets). Monopolistic competition: many firms selling similar but differentiated products (restaurants, clothing brands). Oligopoly: a few large firms dominate — their decisions affect each other (telecom companies, airlines). Monopoly: one firm controls the entire market — can set high prices (utility companies sometimes). More competition generally benefits consumers through lower prices, better quality, and more innovation.
examples: Perfect competition: hundreds of tomato farmers at a market — no single farmer can raise prices above others
Oligopoly: Coca-Cola and Pepsi dominate soft drinks — if one lowers prices, the other responds
Monopoly: if one company controls all water supply in a city, it can charge whatever it wants

keyTerms.monopoly: A market with only one seller — they control the price
keyTerms.oligopoly: A market dominated by a few large firms whose actions affect each other
keyTerms.perfect competition: A market with many small sellers of identical products — no price control

quiz.question: In a monopoly:
options: One firm controls the market and can set prices
quiz.explanation: A monopoly has one seller with no competition — they have pricing power.

quiz.question: Competition benefits consumers through:
quiz.explanation: When firms compete, they lower prices, improve quality, and innovate to win customers.

quiz.question: Telecom companies (MTN, Airtel) represent which market structure?
quiz.explanation: A few large firms dominating a market = oligopoly.

lessons.title: Market Failure and Government Role
lessons.content: Market failure occurs when free markets fail to allocate resources efficiently. Types: externalities (costs or benefits to third parties — factory pollution harms everyone), public goods (goods that are non-excludable and non-rivalrous — street lights, national defense), information asymmetry (one party knows more — used car sellers know defects buyers don't), and monopoly power (one firm exploits consumers). Government responses: taxes (on pollution), subsidies (for education), regulation (safety standards), public provision (government provides healthcare, roads), and competition law (prevents monopolies).
examples: Negative externality: a factory pollutes a river — downstream farmers lose crops, but the factory doesn't pay for this
Public good: a lighthouse benefits all ships — you can't charge each ship, so the government provides it
Government solution: carbon tax makes polluters pay for environmental damage, incentivizing cleaner production

keyTerms.market failure: When free markets fail to allocate resources efficiently for society
keyTerms.externality: A cost or benefit that affects third parties not involved in the transaction
keyTerms.public good: A good that is non-excludable (can't prevent use) and non-rivalrous (one person's use doesn't reduce availability)

quiz.question: Factory pollution is an example of:
quiz.explanation: The pollution costs are imposed on others (third parties) who didn't choose to bear them.

quiz.question: Why can't private markets provide national defense?
options: It's a public good — you can't exclude non-payers
quiz.explanation: Defense protects everyone — you can't exclude people who don't pay, so government provides it.

quiz.question: How can governments address negative externalities?
options: Tax the activity to make polluters pay the true cost
quiz.explanation: Taxes (like carbon tax) make polluters bear the cost, reducing harmful activities.

lessons.title: Elasticity
lessons.content: Elasticity measures how responsive demand or supply is to changes in price. Price elasticity of demand = % change in quantity demanded / % change in price. Elastic demand (>1): a small price change causes a big demand change — luxury goods, things with many substitutes. Inelastic demand (<1): price changes don't affect demand much — necessities, addictive goods, goods with few substitutes. If demand is elastic, raising prices reduces total revenue. If inelastic, raising prices increases revenue. Income elasticity measures how demand changes with income: normal goods (demand rises with income), inferior goods (demand falls as income rises — e.g., switching from bus to taxi).
examples: Elastic: designer handbags — a 10% price increase might cause 30% fewer sales
Inelastic: insulin for diabetics — people need it regardless of price
Inferior good: instant noodles — as income rises, people switch to better food

keyTerms.elastic: Demand changes significantly when price changes (elasticity > 1)
keyTerms.inelastic: Demand changes little when price changes (elasticity < 1)
keyTerms.elasticity: A measure of how responsive quantity demanded/supplied is to price changes

quiz.question: Demand for medicine is typically:
options: Inelastic — people need it regardless of price
quiz.explanation: Essential goods like medicine have inelastic demand — few substitutes and high necessity.

quiz.question: If demand is elastic, raising prices will:
quiz.explanation: Elastic demand means customers are price-sensitive — higher prices drive many away.

quiz.question: An inferior good is one where:
quiz.explanation: As people earn more, they switch to better alternatives — demand for inferior goods drops.

lessons.title: GDP and Economic Growth
lessons.content: GDP (Gross Domestic Product) is the total value of all goods and services produced in a country in a year. It's the main measure of economic size and performance. Real GDP adjusts for inflation; nominal GDP doesn't. GDP per capita = GDP / population — better for comparing living standards between countries. Economic growth means GDP is increasing — more goods, services, jobs, and income. Growth is driven by: investment in capital, technological progress, education (human capital), and institutional quality (rule of law, property rights). Limitations of GDP: it doesn't measure inequality, environmental damage, unpaid work, or wellbeing.
examples: USA GDP: ~$25 trillion. Uganda GDP: ~$45 billion. But Uganda's growth rate (6%) may be faster
GDP per capita: Norway ~$82,000 vs Uganda ~$900 — shows the difference in average income
GDP doesn't count: a parent raising children at home, environmental destruction, or happiness

keyTerms.GDP: Gross Domestic Product — the total value of goods and services produced in a country per year
keyTerms.economic growth: An increase in GDP over time — more production, jobs, and income
keyTerms.GDP per capita: GDP divided by population — a measure of average economic output per person

quiz.question: What does GDP measure?
options: Total value of goods and services produced in a country per year
quiz.explanation: GDP = the monetary value of all final goods and services produced within a country in one year.

quiz.question: GDP per capita is useful for:
quiz.explanation: Dividing GDP by population gives average output per person — a rough living standard indicator.

quiz.question: A limitation of GDP is:
options: It doesn't measure inequality or environmental damage
quiz.explanation: GDP ignores income distribution, environmental costs, unpaid work, and quality of life.

lessons.title: Inflation and Unemployment
lessons.content: Inflation is the general rise in prices over time — your money buys less. Measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI). Moderate inflation (2-3%) is normal and healthy. High inflation (hyperinflation) destroys savings and destabilizes economies — Zimbabwe had 79.6 billion percent monthly inflation in 2008. Causes: demand-pull (too much spending), cost-push (rising input costs), and monetary (too much money printed). Unemployment is the percentage of the labor force without jobs but actively seeking work. Types: frictional (between jobs), structural (skills mismatch), cyclical (due to recession), and seasonal (tourism workers in off-season).
examples: If inflation is 10%, something that cost 1,000 last year now costs 1,100
Zimbabwe 2008: prices doubled every 24 hours — people needed wheelbarrows of cash to buy bread
Structural unemployment: coal miners lose jobs because the economy shifts to solar energy — their skills don't transfer easily

keyTerms.inflation: A general sustained rise in the price level, reducing the purchasing power of money
keyTerms.CPI: Consumer Price Index — measures the average change in prices of a basket of goods over time
keyTerms.unemployment rate: The percentage of the labor force that is jobless and actively seeking work

quiz.question: Inflation means:
options: Prices are generally rising — money buys less
quiz.explanation: Inflation = sustained rise in the general price level, reducing purchasing power.

quiz.question: A healthy inflation rate is about:
quiz.explanation: Most economists consider 2-3% inflation healthy for a growing economy.

quiz.question: Structural unemployment is caused by:
options: A mismatch between workers' skills and available jobs
quiz.explanation: When industries change, workers' old skills may not match new job requirements.

lessons.title: Government Economic Policy
lessons.content: Governments use two main policy tools. Fiscal policy: adjusting government spending and taxation. In a recession, the government increases spending and cuts taxes to boost demand (expansionary). To cool an overheating economy, it reduces spending and raises taxes (contractionary). Monetary policy: the central bank adjusts interest rates and money supply. Lower interest rates encourage borrowing and spending. Higher rates discourage borrowing and slow inflation. A government budget deficit means it spends more than it collects in taxes (borrows the difference). National debt is the accumulated total of all past deficits.
examples: Fiscal: during COVID-19, governments sent money to citizens and businesses to prevent economic collapse
Monetary: when inflation is high, the central bank raises interest rates to reduce spending
Budget deficit: government earns 10 trillion in taxes but spends 12 trillion — borrows 2 trillion

keyTerms.fiscal policy: Government adjusting spending and taxation to influence the economy
keyTerms.monetary policy: Central bank adjusting interest rates and money supply to control inflation and growth
keyTerms.budget deficit: When government spending exceeds tax revenue in a given period

quiz.question: To fight a recession, the government should:
quiz.explanation: Expansionary fiscal policy boosts demand by putting more money in the economy.

quiz.question: Raising interest rates helps reduce:
quiz.explanation: Higher rates discourage borrowing and spending, reducing demand and slowing price increases.

quiz.question: A budget deficit means:
options: Government spends more than it earns in taxes
Government earns more than it spends
quiz.explanation: Deficit = spending > revenue. The government borrows to cover the gap.

lessons.title: Money and Banking
lessons.content: Money serves three functions: medium of exchange (you trade money for goods instead of bartering), store of value (you can save it for later), and unit of account (prices are measured in money). Banks accept deposits, make loans, and facilitate payments. When a bank makes a loan, it effectively creates new money — this is how the money supply expands. Central banks (Bank of Uganda, Federal Reserve, Bank of England) regulate the banking system, set interest rates, and control money supply. Mobile money (M-Pesa, MTN Mobile Money) has revolutionized banking in Africa — providing financial services to people without bank accounts.
examples: Before money, people bartered: trading a goat for 10 bags of grain — but what if the grain seller didn't want a goat?
Fractional reserve banking: a bank keeps 10% of deposits and lends 90% — deposits multiply through the system
M-Pesa processes over $300 billion in transactions annually — more than many traditional banks

keyTerms.medium of exchange: Money's role as something accepted in transactions for goods and services
keyTerms.central bank: The institution that manages a country's currency, money supply, and interest rates
keyTerms.mobile money: Financial services delivered through mobile phones, enabling payments and transfers

quiz.question: Money serves as a:
options: Medium of exchange, store of value, and unit of account
quiz.explanation: Money has three functions: you trade it, save it, and use it to measure prices.

quiz.question: What is the role of a central bank?
options: Regulate banks, set interest rates, control money supply
quiz.explanation: Central banks manage the monetary system — they don't serve individual customers.

quiz.question: Mobile money has been revolutionary because:
options: It provides financial services to people without bank accounts
quiz.explanation: Mobile money gives unbanked populations access to payments, savings, and transfers.

lessons.title: International Trade
lessons.content: International trade is the exchange of goods and services between countries. Countries trade because of comparative advantage — each country produces what it can make most efficiently and trades for the rest. Exports are goods sold to other countries; imports are goods bought from other countries. The balance of trade is exports minus imports. Free trade removes barriers (tariffs, quotas). Protectionism uses barriers to protect domestic industries. The World Trade Organization (WTO) sets global trade rules. Trade blocs (EU, African Continental Free Trade Area) reduce barriers between member countries.
examples: Uganda exports coffee and tea (comparative advantage in agriculture) and imports electronics and machinery
A tariff: Uganda charges 25% tax on imported sugar to protect domestic sugar producers
The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) aims to create a single market of 1.3 billion people across Africa

keyTerms.comparative advantage: A country's ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than others
keyTerms.tariff: A tax on imported goods, making them more expensive to protect domestic producers
keyTerms.balance of trade: The difference between the value of a country's exports and imports

quiz.question: Countries trade because of:
options: Comparative advantage — each produces what it does best
quiz.explanation: Trade lets countries specialize in what they're most efficient at producing.

quiz.question: A tariff is:
quiz.explanation: Tariffs make imports more expensive, protecting domestic producers from foreign competition.

quiz.question: AfCFTA aims to:
options: Create a single African market of 1.3 billion people
quiz.explanation: The African Continental Free Trade Area reduces trade barriers across Africa.

lessons.title: Exchange Rates and Development
lessons.content: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another. If 1 USD = 3,700 UGX, a $10 item costs 37,000 UGX. Floating exchange rates are determined by supply and demand. If a country exports a lot, demand for its currency rises, making it stronger (appreciates). Economic development is broader than growth — it includes improvements in health, education, living standards, and equality. Measured by the Human Development Index (HDI) which combines income, life expectancy, and education. Developing countries face challenges: poverty, limited infrastructure, brain drain, and debt. Aid, trade, investment, and good governance all play roles in development.
examples: Exchange rate change: if UGX weakens from 3,700 to 4,000 per USD, imports become more expensive for Ugandans
HDI rankings: Norway (very high), Uganda (medium) — HDI is a better measure of wellbeing than GDP alone
Microfinance: small loans to entrepreneurs in developing countries — helps people start businesses and escape poverty

keyTerms.exchange rate: The price of one currency expressed in terms of another currency
keyTerms.HDI: Human Development Index — measures development using income, life expectancy, and education
keyTerms.economic development: Improvements in living standards, health, education, and equality — broader than GDP growth

quiz.question: If UGX weakens against USD, imports become:
quiz.explanation: A weaker currency means you need more shillings to buy the same dollar amount of imports.

quiz.question: HDI measures:
options: Income, life expectancy, and education combined
quiz.explanation: HDI gives a broader picture of development than GDP alone.

quiz.question: Economic development includes:
options: Improvements in health, education, and living standards
quiz.explanation: Development goes beyond growth — it includes quality of life, equity, and human wellbeing.
